title: How many digits does a product have? Find the rule
description: The digit counts in the rows of the table are read for a pattern, and the pattern is explained with two numbers of two digits. The rule then fills three empty rows. Keeko then raises a hand, thinking the product always has the sum of the digit counts.
teaching_notes: One idea: the product has the sum of the digit counts, or one less. Ask the class to add the digit counts in the first three rows of the table before the pattern is named. Watch for students who say the product always has exactly the sum of the digit counts.

source: Observe the multiplication statements below. Do you notice any patterns? See if this pattern extends for other numbers as well.
video_script.why: The child has found the digit counts of products of two and three digit numbers, and now sees the rule that works for any digit counts.
video_script.substitution: Add the digit counts of the two numbers, the product has that many digits or one less.
video_script.anchor: A table of digit counts: 1-digit × 1-digit = 1 or 2, 2-digit × 1-digit = 2 or 3, 2-digit × 2-digit = 3 or 4, 3-digit × 3-digit = 5 or 6, and three empty rows.
video_script.wrong_answer: exactly the sum of the digit counts
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the product has exactly the sum of the digit counts. But 10 × 10 = 100 has 3 digits, one less than 2 + 2.
video_script.payoff_line: The product has the sum of the digit counts, or one less

final_answer.value: 9 or 10; 10 or 11; 24 or 25 digits. The rule is m + n − 1 or m + n digits
final_answer.spoken: nine or ten digits, ten or eleven digits, twenty four or twenty five digits, and the rule is the sum of the digit counts or one fewer

never_show: the digit counts of the 12-digit times 13-digit row before the answer beat
maths_rules: rows: 1 + 1 = 2 gives 1 or 2; 2 + 1 = 3 gives 2 or 3; 2 + 2 = 4 gives 3 or 4; 3 + 3 = 6 gives 5 or 6; each is the sum or one less
why: 10 × 10 = 100 has 3 = 2 + 2 − 1 digits; every product is below 100 × 100 = 10,000, which has 5 digits, so at most 4 = 2 + 2
rule: an m-digit number times an n-digit number has m + n − 1 or m + n digits
video_script.design: One idea: the digit count of a product is the sum of the digit counts, or one less. Wrong idea: Keeko says it is exactly the sum. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, see why with two digits times two digits. The smallest product is ten times ten, which is one hundred, with three digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Every product is below one hundred times one hundred, which is ten thousand, with five digits.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The count is two plus two minus one, or two plus two.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, five digits times five digits. The sum is ten, and one less is nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eight digits times three digits. The sum is eleven, and one less is ten.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Twelve digits times thirteen digits. The sum is twenty five, and one less is twenty four.
